stem:
Consider the sets
\(\phi\), \(A = \{ 1, 3 \}\), \(B = \{1, 5, 9\}\), \(C = \{1, 3, 5, 7, 9\}\).
Insert the symbol \(\subset\) or \(\not\subset\) between each of the following pair of sets:
(i) \(\phi \ldots B\)  (ii) \(A \ldots B\)  (iii) \(A \ldots C\)  (iv) \(B \ldots C\)
solution:
(i) \(\phi \subset B\) as \(\phi\) is a subset of every set.
(ii) \(A \not\subset B\) as \(3 \in A\) and \(3 \notin B\)
(iii) \(A \subset C\) as \(1, 3 \in A\) also belongs to \(C\)
(iv) \(B \subset C\) as each element of \(B\) is also an element of \(C\).

stem: Let \(A = \{ a, e, i, o, u\}\) and \(B = \{ a, b, c, d\}\). Is \(A\) a subset of \(B\) ? No. (Why?). Is \(B\) a subset of \(A\)? No. (Why?)
_note: NO PRINTED SOLUTION BLOCK. The book gives this Example no "Solution" heading at all — the verdicts ("No") are embedded in the stem as rhetorical questions and the reasons are left to the reader as "(Why?)". The `solution` field is deliberately omitted rather than invented; the outstanding question is the two "Why?" justifications.

stem: Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be three sets. If \(A \in B\) and \(B \subset C\), is it true that \(A \subset C\)?. If not, give an example.
solution:
No. Let \(A = \{1\}\), \(B = \{\{1\}, 2\}\) and \(C = \{\{1\}, 2, 3\}\). Here \(A \in B\) as \(A = \{1\}\) and \(B \subset C\). But \(A \not\subset C\) as \(1 \in A\) and \(1 \notin C\).
Note that an element of a set can never be a subset of itself.
_note: The book prints the stem's question mark before the full stop — "is it true that A \(\subset\) C?." — transcribed as printed. The closing line "Note that an element of a set can never be a subset of itself." is INCLUDED IN THE SOLUTION: it is set flush to the solution block's left margin with no paragraph indent, immediately after the last solution line, and the next indented paragraph is the \(\S\)1.6.1 heading. It reads as the solution's closing remark rather than as fresh chapter prose.

stem: Let \(A = \{ a, e, i, o, u \}\) and \(B = \{ a, i, u \}\). Show that \(A \cup B = A\).
solution:
We have, \(A \cup B = \{ a, e, i, o, u \} = A\).
This example illustrates that union of sets \(A\) and its subset \(B\) is the set \(A\) itself, i.e., if \(B \subset A\), then \(A \cup B = A\).

solution:
We have, \(V - B = \{ e, o \}\), since the elements \(e, o\) belong to \(V\) but not to \(B\) and \(B - V = \{ k \}\), since the element \(k\) belongs to \(B\) but not to \(V\).

stem: Show that the set of letters needed to spell " CATARACT " and the set of letters needed to spell " TRACT" are equal.
solution:
Let \(X\) be the set of letters in "CATARACT". Then \(X = \{ C, A, T, R \}\).
Let \(Y\) be the set of letters in " TRACT". Then \(Y = \{ T, R, A, C, T \} = \{ T, R, A, C \}\).
Since every element in \(X\) is in \(Y\) and every element in \(Y\) is in \(X\). It follows that \(X = Y\).

stem: List all the subsets of the set \(\{ -1, 0, 1 \}\).
solution: Let \(A = \{ -1, 0, 1 \}\). The subset of \(A\) having no element is the empty set \(\phi\). The subsets of \(A\) having one element are \(\{ -1 \}\), \(\{ 0 \}\), \(\{ 1 \}\). The subsets of \(A\) having two elements are \(\{-1, 0\}\), \(\{-1, 1\}\), \(\{0, 1\}\). The subset of \(A\) having three elements of \(A\) is \(A\) itself. So, all the subsets of \(A\) are \(\phi\), \(\{-1\}\), \(\{0\}\), \(\{1\}\), \(\{-1, 0\}\), \(\{-1, 1\}\), \(\{0, 1\}\) and \(\{-1, 0, 1\}\).

subtopic: Venn Diagrams and Operations on Sets
stem: Show that \(A \cup B = A \cap B\) implies \(A = B\).
solution:
Let \(a \in A\). Then \(a \in A \cup B\). Since \(A \cup B = A \cap B\), \(a \in A \cap B\). So \(a \in B\). Therefore, \(A \subset B\).
Similarly, if \(b \in B\), then \(b \in A \cup B\). Since \(A \cup B = A \cap B\), \(b \in A \cap B\). So, \(b \in A\). Therefore, \(B \subset A\).
Thus, \(A = B\).
